cards.title: Tree Fundamentals
cards.teaser: A tree is a connected, acyclic graph of nodes linked by edges. The root is the single top node, leaves have no children, depth measures distance from the root, and height measures the longest path down — these terms appear in every tree algorithm.

runs.text: A
tree

is a hierarchical data structure where each node stores a value and zero or more references to child nodes. Unlike a general graph, a tree has no cycles and has exactly one path between any two nodes. The key vocabulary:

items.text: — the single top-level node with no parent.
— if node A points to node B, A is B's parent and B is A's child.
— number of edges from the root to that node. The root has depth 0.
— number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf.
— any node together with all of its descendants; a tree is recursively defined by its subtrees.

explanation.code:
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val: int):
        self.val = val
        self.children: list['TreeNode'] = []

# A tree with root 1, children 2 and 3, grandchild 4:
#       1          ← root, depth 0
#      / \
#     2   3        ← depth 1
#    /
#   4              ← leaf, depth 2; tree height = 2

runs.text: Trees model hierarchical data naturally: file systems (directories as internal nodes, files as leaves), HTML DOM (document root, element children), organizational charts, and recursive algorithms. Most of the specialized trees you'll encounter — BSTs, heaps, tries — are just trees with additional ordering or shape constraints layered on top.
A tree with n nodes always has exactly n − 1 edges. Adding one more edge creates a cycle and makes it a general graph.

A tree is a family tree for data: one root at the top, each node has children below it, and no node has two parents. Depth counts how many steps down from the root a node sits; height counts the longest path from root to a leaf at the bottom.

cards.title: Binary Tree
cards.teaser: A binary tree restricts each node to at most two children, called left and right. This simple constraint is the foundation for BSTs, heaps, expression trees, and most tree algorithms — at most 2 children means at most 2 recursive calls.

runs.text: A
binary tree
is a tree where every node has at most two children, conventionally labeled
left
and
right
. Either or both can be
None
. This two-branch structure maps directly onto recursive algorithms: process the left subtree, process the right subtree, combine.

explanation.code:
class BinaryTreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val: int,
                 left: 'BinaryTreeNode | None' = None,
                 right: 'BinaryTreeNode | None' = None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

# Build:   4
#         / \
#        2   6
#       / \
#      1   3
root = BinaryTreeNode(4,
    left=BinaryTreeNode(2,
        left=BinaryTreeNode(1),
        right=BinaryTreeNode(3)),
    right=BinaryTreeNode(6))

runs.text: Key shape classifications:

items.text: — all levels are full except possibly the last, which is filled left-to-right. Heaps use this shape.
— every level is completely full. A perfect tree of height h has 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes.
— every node has only one child; structurally a linked list. Height = n − 1.

runs.text: A balanced binary tree of n nodes has height O(log n), so operations that walk root-to-leaf are O(log n). A degenerate tree degrades those same operations to O(n).

A binary tree is just a tree where every node can have at most two children — a left one and a right one. That simple rule is what lets you write recursive algorithms with exactly two recursive calls, one per subtree.

cards.title: Binary Search Tree (BST)
cards.teaser: A BST is a binary tree with an ordering invariant: every value in a node's left subtree is smaller, and every value in its right subtree is larger. This invariant enables O(log n) search, insert, and delete on a balanced tree.

runs.text: A
Binary Search Tree (BST)
enforces the
BST property

at every node: all values in the left subtree are strictly less than the node's value, and all values in the right subtree are strictly greater. This ordering means search works exactly like binary search on a sorted array — at each node, you eliminate half the remaining tree.

explanation.code:
# Valid BST:
#        8
#       / \
#      3   10
#     / \    \
#    1   6    14
#       / \
#      4   7
# For node 3: left subtree {1} < 3 < {4, 6, 7} right subtree ✓
# For node 8: left subtree {1,3,4,6,7} < 8 < {10,14} right subtree ✓

def search(node, target):
    if node is None or node.val == target:
        return node
    if target < node.val:
        return search(node.left, target)   # go left
    return search(node.right, target)      # go right

runs.text: The BST property has a critical consequence for in-order traversal: visiting nodes left → root → right produces values in sorted ascending order. This makes a BST an efficient sorted container — you can iterate all values in O(n) time, or find any value in O(log n) time (when balanced).

The BST property must hold for the entire subtree, not just immediate children. It is a common mistake to verify only parent-child pairs. Use min/max bounds propagated top-down to validate a BST correctly.

A BST is a binary tree with a rule: everything to the left of a node is smaller, everything to the right is larger. That rule lets you search like a phone book — at each node you ask 'too big or too small?' and throw away half the tree until you find it.

cards.title: BST Operations: Insert, Search, Delete
cards.teaser: BST insert and search are O(log n) on a balanced tree and O(n) on a skewed one. Delete has three cases: leaf (just remove), one child (bypass), two children (replace with in-order successor then delete successor). Balance is everything.

runs.text: All three core BST operations walk from root toward a leaf, taking O(h) time where h is the tree's height. On a balanced tree h = O(log n); on a degenerate tree h = O(n).
The delete two-children case is the trickiest. The
in-order successor

is the smallest value in the right subtree — found by going right once then left as far as possible. Overwriting the deleted node's value with the successor's value, then deleting the successor, preserves the BST property because the successor is larger than everything in the left subtree and smaller than everything else in the right subtree.

Inserting a sorted sequence into an unbalanced BST creates a degenerate tree with height n — every insert goes right. AVL and Red-Black trees solve this by rebalancing automatically after insert and delete.

BST insert just walks down and hangs the new value at the right spot. Search walks down comparing at each node. Delete is the messy one: a leaf is trivial to remove, a node with one child gets bypassed, and a node with two children gets replaced by its in-order successor — the next-bigger value in the tree.

cards.title: Tree Traversals: In-Order, Pre-Order, Post-Order
cards.teaser: DFS traversals visit every node exactly once in O(n). In-order (left → root → right) yields sorted output from a BST. Pre-order (root → left → right) serializes a tree. Post-order (left → right → root) evaluates expression trees. The order of the recursive calls determines everything.

runs.text: Depth-first traversals differ only in
when
you process the current node relative to its subtrees. All three visit every node exactly once, so all are O(n) time and O(h) space for the call stack.

explanation.code:
def inorder(node, result=[]):
    """Left → Root → Right. Yields sorted order from a BST."""
    if node:
        inorder(node.left, result)
        result.append(node.val)   # ← process here
        inorder(node.right, result)

def preorder(node, result=[]):
    """Root → Left → Right. Good for copying/serializing a tree."""
    if node:
        result.append(node.val)   # ← process here
        preorder(node.left, result)
        preorder(node.right, result)

def postorder(node, result=[]):
    """Left → Right → Root. Good for deleting or evaluating a tree."""
    if node:
        postorder(node.left, result)
        postorder(node.right, result)
        result.append(node.val)   # ← process here

# For the tree:  4 / 2 \ 6 with 2's children 1 and 3:
# inorder  → [1, 2, 3, 4, 6]  (sorted!)
# preorder → [4, 2, 1, 3, 6]  (root first)
# postorder→ [1, 3, 2, 6, 4]  (root last)

runs.text: Use cases by traversal type:

items.text: — produce sorted output from a BST; validate BST property by checking the sequence is ascending.
— serialize a tree (the root comes first, so deserialization knows where to start); copy a tree structure.
— evaluate expression trees (children before parent); safely delete a tree (children before parent frees memory correctly).

runs.text: A mnemonic: the name describes where the root lands relative to its children — pre (root first), in (root between), post (root last).

The three DFS traversals are the same recursive algorithm with one line moved. Move the 'process node' step before the recursive calls and you get pre-order. Put it between the calls and you get in-order. Put it after and you get post-order. The order of that single step changes everything about what order you see the values.

cards.title: Level-Order Traversal (BFS on Trees)
cards.teaser: Level-order traversal visits nodes row by row, top to bottom, using a queue instead of recursion. It's BFS applied to a tree and is the go-to approach for problems that ask about tree width, minimum depth, or right-side view.

runs.text: Level-order traversal visits every node at depth
d
before any node at depth
. It uses a
queue
(FIFO) rather than a stack or the call stack, which is the fundamental difference from DFS traversals. Time and space complexity are both O(n).
The
level_size snapshot

trick — capturing the queue length before processing a level — is the standard way to separate nodes by depth within a single BFS loop. Without it you'd process all nodes in flat order without knowing when one level ends and the next begins.

Problems that level-order solves cleanly: right-side view (take the last element of each level), zigzag traversal (alternate left-to-right and right-to-left per level), minimum depth (first level that contains a leaf), and connecting nodes at the same level.
BFS on a tree is guaranteed to terminate and visit each node once. Unlike BFS on a general graph, you don't need a visited set — trees have no cycles.

Level-order traversal is like reading a tree floor by floor. You use a queue: put the root in, then in each iteration dequeue a node, record its value, and enqueue its children. Because a queue is FIFO, children get processed after all their siblings — that's what keeps everything level-by-level.

cards.title: AVL Tree
cards.teaser: An AVL tree is a self-balancing BST that keeps the heights of any node's left and right subtrees within 1. After every insert or delete, it restores balance with rotations. This guarantees O(log n) worst-case for all operations.

runs.text: Georgy Adelson-Velsky and Evgenii Landis invented the AVL tree in 1962 — the first self-balancing BST. The
balance factor
of a node is defined as height(left subtree) − height(right subtree). AVL trees enforce: every node's balance factor must be −1, 0, or +1 at all times.

explanation.code:
# The four rotation cases that restore AVL balance:
#
# Left-Left (LL): right-rotate at the imbalanced node
#     z              y
#    /              / \
#   y      →       x   z
#  /
# x
#
# Right-Right (RR): left-rotate at the imbalanced node
# z                  y
#  \                / \
#   y      →       z   x
#    \
#     x
#
# Left-Right (LR): left-rotate y, then right-rotate z
# Right-Left (RL): right-rotate y, then left-rotate z

def height(node):
    return node.height if node else -1

def balance_factor(node):
    return height(node.left) - height(node.right)

runs.text: After an insert or delete, the algorithm walks back up the tree checking balance factors. When it finds a node with |balance factor| = 2, it applies one of four rotation patterns (LL, RR, LR, RL) to restore balance in O(1) time. The tree is then guaranteed to have height ≤ 1.44 log₂(n + 2) — very close to the theoretical minimum of log₂ n.

AVL trees are more strictly balanced than Red-Black trees, so lookups are slightly faster. But AVL trees require more rotations on average during insert/delete. This makes Red-Black trees preferable in write-heavy workloads (e.g., C++ std::map, Java TreeMap).

An AVL tree is a BST that checks its own balance after every insert or delete. It measures how lopsided each node's subtrees are (the balance factor) and performs rotations — tree restructurings that take O(1) — to fix any imbalance. The result is always a near-perfectly balanced tree with O(log n) height.

cards.title: Red-Black Tree
cards.teaser: A Red-Black tree is a self-balancing BST where every node is colored red or black and five coloring rules guarantee the tree stays within a 2× factor of optimal height. It's the backbone of Java's TreeMap, C++'s std::map, and Linux's process scheduler.

runs.text: A
Red-Black tree
maintains balance through five properties:

items.text: Every node is red or black.
If a node is red, both its children are black (no two consecutive reds).
All paths from any node to its descendant nil leaves contain the same number of black nodes (the black-height is uniform).

runs.text: These rules together bound the height: the longest root-to-leaf path (alternating red and black nodes) can be at most twice the shortest path (all black nodes). So height ≤ 2 log₂(n + 1), giving O(log n) worst-case for all operations.
Rebalancing after insert or delete uses a combination of
recoloring
(change a node's color) and
rotations
(same left/right rotations as AVL). Crucially, Red-Black trees require at most 2 rotations per insert and 3 per delete — AVL can require O(log n) rebalancing steps per delete.

Python's sortedcontainers.SortedList and Java's TreeMap are backed by Red-Black trees. In Python's CPython source, the scheduler and memory allocator use similar balanced BST ideas. You rarely implement a Red-Black tree — you use one from a library — but understanding the properties lets you reason about its guarantees.

A Red-Black tree is a BST where every node is painted red or black and five color rules keep the tree balanced without being as strict as AVL. The key rule: no two red nodes in a row, and all root-to-leaf paths have the same number of black nodes. These rules guarantee height at most 2 log n — close enough to optimal for all operations to stay O(log n).

cards.title: B-Tree and B+ Tree
cards.teaser: A B-tree generalizes the BST to nodes with many keys and many children, minimizing disk I/O by keeping the tree shallow. B+ trees add a linked leaf layer for fast range scans. Both are the dominant index structure in databases and filesystems.

runs.text: B-trees were designed for storage systems where reading a single disk block costs far more than in-memory comparisons. By packing many keys into one node (matching the block size), a B-tree of order
t
keeps its height to O(log_t n), so most lookups require only 2–4 disk reads even for billions of records.

explanation.code:
# B-tree of order t (min degree):
# - Every non-root node has at least t-1 keys and at most 2t-1 keys.
# - A node with k keys has k+1 children (for internal nodes).
# - All leaves are at the same depth.
#
# Example B-tree (t=2, so 1–3 keys per node):
#
#          [10 | 20]
#         /    |    \
#       [5]  [15]  [25 | 30]
#
# Lookup 15: read root → 10 < 15 < 20 → go to middle child → found
# Only 2 disk reads for the entire search.

runs.text: A
B+ tree
adds one critical constraint: all actual data (or record pointers) live only in
leaf nodes

, which are linked together in a doubly-linked list. Internal nodes store only keys for routing. This gives two advantages: internal nodes fit more keys (higher branching factor, shorter tree), and range queries scan the leaf chain without going back up the tree.

items.text: — use B+ trees for both primary keys and secondary indexes.
— use B-tree variants for directory structures.
— uses B+ trees for its default storage engine.

runs.text: LSM trees (Log-Structured Merge-trees, used in RocksDB, Cassandra, LevelDB) are the main alternative to B+ trees for write-heavy workloads — they batch writes in memory and merge sorted runs sequentially, trading random writes for sequential I/O.

A B-tree is a BST that got wider instead of taller. Each node holds many keys and has many children, matching the size of a disk block. Fewer levels means fewer disk reads. A B+ tree goes one step further: only leaf nodes hold data, and those leaves are linked like a list, so range queries — 'give me all rows between 100 and 200' — just scan the leaf chain without touching internal nodes.

cards.title: Trie (Prefix Tree)
cards.teaser: A trie stores strings by their characters along root-to-leaf paths. Every node represents a prefix; children represent the next character. Lookup, insert, and prefix search are all O(L) where L is the string length — independent of how many strings are stored.

runs.text: A
trie
(pronounced "try", from re
trie
val) stores a set of strings by sharing common prefixes. Each edge is labeled with a character; each node represents the string formed by the edge labels from root to that node. A special
is_end
flag marks nodes where a complete word terminates.

All operations run in O(L) time where L is the string length — no comparison with other stored strings is needed. Space is O(total characters), which can be large. Compressed tries (radix trees / Patricia trees) merge chains of single-child nodes to reduce space.

Tries power autocomplete (type 'app', get 'apple', 'application'), spell checkers, IP routing tables, and dictionary word-break problems. They are the natural structure whenever prefix relationships matter.
A set of n strings with average length L takes O(n × L) space in a trie. For dense character sets (e.g., Unicode), use a dict of children per node rather than a fixed-size array of 26 slots.

A trie is a tree where each edge is a character. You insert a word by following one edge per letter, creating nodes as needed. To look up a word, follow the same edges — if you can, and the last node is marked as a word ending, the word is in the trie. Prefix search is free: just follow the prefix and everything below that node is a match.

cards.title: Segment Tree
cards.teaser: A segment tree answers range queries (sum, min, max) in O(log n) and supports point updates in O(log n). It builds a binary tree where each node stores the aggregate of a range, halving the range at each level — divide-and-conquer made persistent.

runs.text: A
segment tree

precomputes and stores aggregate values (sum, min, max, GCD, etc.) for every contiguous subarray, organized in a binary tree. The root stores the aggregate of the full array; the left and right children store the aggregates of the left and right halves; leaves store individual elements. The tree has 4n nodes in the worst case.
A naive approach to range sum queries takes O(n) per query and O(1) per update (just modify the array). A prefix sum array makes queries O(1) but updates O(n). The segment tree achieves O(log n) for
both
query and update, at the cost of O(n) build time and O(n) space.
Lazy propagation extends the segment tree to support range updates (e.g., add 5 to all elements in arr[l..r]) in O(log n) by deferring the update to children until they are queried.

A segment tree precomputes sums (or mins or maxes) for every possible contiguous subarray and stores them in a binary tree. When you ask for the sum of arr[3..7], it decomposes the range into a handful of precomputed segments and adds them — O(log n) instead of O(n). When you update one element, it fixes only the O(log n) tree nodes that cover that position.

cards.title: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
cards.teaser: A Fenwick tree answers prefix sum queries and point updates in O(log n) with a simpler implementation than a segment tree. Each index stores a partial sum over a range determined by the lowest set bit — clever bit manipulation replaces explicit tree pointers.

runs.text: A
Fenwick tree
(also called a Binary Indexed Tree or BIT) is a 1-indexed array where each position
i
stores the sum of elements from index
i − lowbit(i) + 1
to
i
, where
lowbit(i) = i & (-i)
extracts the lowest set bit. Navigating the tree up or down is done by adding or stripping this lowest bit.

Compared to a segment tree: the Fenwick tree uses exactly n+1 integers (vs ~4n), has shorter and faster code, and is faster in practice due to better cache behavior. Its limitation is that it natively supports only operations whose inverse exists (sum/subtract, XOR) — range-minimum queries require the segment tree instead.

items.text: when you need prefix sums or point updates and want minimal code and memory.
when you need range min/max, non-invertible operations, or range updates with lazy propagation.

runs.text: The bit trick i & (-i) isolates the lowest set bit because -i in two's complement flips all bits above the lowest set bit, so ANDing keeps only that bit. This single expression is the entire navigation logic of a Fenwick tree.

A Fenwick tree is a plain array that acts like a tree using bit tricks. Each position stores a partial sum covering a range whose length is determined by the lowest set bit of the index. To get a prefix sum you hop to smaller indexes by stripping that bit; to update you hop to larger indexes by adding it. Two while loops, each running O(log n) times, and you've replaced a full segment tree with a single array.
